Quasi-one-dimensional taco-shaped bands in large-angle twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides

Giovanny Espitia1∗    Seung Hun Lee1∗    Calvin Kaiyu Chiu1    Junyeong Ahn1† and Mit H. Naik1†
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Two-dimensional moiré materials offer a powerful, twist-tunable platform for engineering electronic bands and correlations, though most studies to date have focused on small twist angles where flat bands arise from symmetry-pinned monolayer momenta. Here, we observe the surprising emergence of flat electronic bands with a distinctive quasi-one-dimensional dispersion at large twist angles in bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides that originate from the Λ\Lambda valley states at generic momenta between Γ\Gamma and KK points. These taco-shaped anisotropic bands result from optimal interlayer hybridization between like-spin Λ\Lambda valleys at the conduction band minimum in the Brillouin zone, resulting in directional band flattening at a magic twist-angle of 21.8∘. The bands form six anisotropic channels with a sixfold alternating spin texture reminiscent of altermagnetic textures. At low energies, the density of states shows a power-law dependence due to the quasi-one-dimensional character, enhancing the potential for correlated phases. Our results provide a new platform for correlated phenomena and broaden the scope of moiré engineering to large twist angles in 2D materials.

Materials whose electronic dispersion contains flat bands are interesting due to their ability to host correlated phases of matter that lead to phenomena such as unconventional superconductivity [10, 9, 33, 65, 69], quantum anomalous Hall effect [8, 48, 68, 40, 36], and generalized Wigner crystalizations [32, 49, 34]. A versatile way to engineer such bands is to form a moiré superlattice by rotating one two-dimensional layer relative to another [12]. The prototypical case is twisted bilayer graphene, where a series of small “magic” angles generate flat bands near the Fermi level [1, 3, 11]. More recently, twisted bilayers of transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have exhibited analogous correlated behavior at small twist angles [16, 45, 39]. So far, most studies have focused on flat bands [31], correlated states [32, 49, 35, 8, 65, 66, 64], and novel moiré excitons [57, 47, 1, 53, 33, 23] at small twist angles in transition metal dichalcogenides driven by structural reconstructions and inhomogeneous interlayer hybridization in large-area moiré superlattices [45, 46]. Despite these rich phenomena, a common limitation of small-angle moiré superlattices is their strong sample heterogeneity [58, 35] and sensitivity to sample preparation. This arises from their tendency toward domain-wall formation and disorder [58, 55, 61, 35], induced by substantial structural reconstructions driven by the strongly varying generalized stacking-fault energy landscape [13, 19]. In contrast, large-angle moiré superlattices are more robust against layer misalignment and manifest less disorder due to reduced structural relaxation [42, 37, 38], offering a promising route to combine enhanced stability with the tunability of moiré engineering.

Large twist angles in TMDs, however, have received little attention, since flat bands do not arise from simple moiré hybridization of high-symmetry-point valleys in this regime. The most studied valley in transition metal dichalcogenides is at the KK point in the Brillouin zone. The valence and conduction band extrema at the KK valleys originate primarily from transition-metal dd orbitals, resulting in wavefunctions that are highly confined within individual layers and exhibit weak interlayer hybridization [32, 44, 7]. At large twist angles, the substantial momentum mismatch between the KK valleys of the two layers leads to nearly layer-degenerate states at the band edges and small gap openings appear at valley crossing points at energies farther from the valence and conduction band edges. At small twist angles, the Γ\Gamma valleys in the valence band exhibit significant interlayer hybridization and are strongly affected by the varying interlayer spacing in the superlattice [46, 2]. On the other hand, at large twist angles, since the interlayer spacing shows no variation, the Γ\Gamma valleys do not host any flat bands. The emergence of flat bands at large twist angles in bilayers has only recently been realized using approaches that go beyond conventional moiré superlattice formation, employing super-moiré structures [37], namely, large-scale moiré-of-moiré structures formed at small deviations from commensurate angles.

In this work, we demonstrate a new mechanism for the emergence of a flat-band dispersion in a class of large-angle TMDs, realized without relying on lattice reconstructions. In most natural bilayer TMDs (MoS2, MoSe2, WS2, WSe2), the conduction band minimum (CBM) lies at the Λ\Lambda valley of the Brillouin zone, located approximately midway between the high-symmetry Γ\Gamma and KK points [7, 52]. The conduction-band wavefunctions at the Λ\Lambda valley exhibit stronger interlayer hybridization compared to the valence and conduction band KK valleys owing to their substantial out-of-plane extent, arising from dominant Se-pzp_{z} orbital character [44, 52]. In this work, we investigate the emergent electronic phenomena that arise when the relative separation between these valleys is tuned by twisting the layers. Our first-principles calculations and theoretical model reveal the emergence of a unique flat band with a taco-shaped quasi-one-dimensional dispersion in large-angle twisted bilayer TMDs. The flat band originates from optimal interlayer hybridization between like-spin Λ\Lambda valleys at the CBM of the Brillouin zone. The emergent flat band consists of six elongated valleys connected across the moiré Brillouin zone, forming quasi-one-dimensional electronic pathways with alternating spin polarization under sixfold rotation, reminiscent of altermagnetic spin textures. The reduced dimensionality of these bands produces a power-law divergent density of states, potentially promoting strong electronic interactions and correlated behavior.

This band flattening is driven by a delicate interplay between the interlayer coupling strength and the spin texture of adjacent Λ\Lambda valleys of opposite layers, which align optimally only at the specific twist angle of 21.8∘. At this ”magic” angle, the interlayer hybridization is sufficiently strong as well as spin-compatible to produce a remarkably flat band connecting the adjacent Λ\Lambda valleys in the Brillouin zone (BZ). Even small departure from this angle rapidly disrupts the alignment of the Λ\Lambda valleys, removing the conditions necessary for flat-band formation. While strong interlayer coupling through Umklapp scattering at commensurate twist angles, such as 21.8∘, has been reported in graphene bilayers [5], we emphasize that the magic angle here does not arise solely from enhanced hybridization.

Directional band flattening at 21.8∘ twist

First, we describe the origin of the flat bands that emerge from the Λ\Lambda valley. Fig. 1a shows the simulated 21.8∘ moiré unit cell in real space. At this commensurate twist angle, the resulting moiré superlattice is a 7×7\sqrt{7}\times\sqrt{7} supercell relative to the primitive unit cell. The individual BZs of the top and bottom WSe2 layers are shown in Fig. 1b and Fig. 1c; where the central smaller hexagon is the common moiré BZ onto which the individual layer k-points fold into at a twist angle of 21.8∘21.8^{\circ} and 38.2∘38.2^{\circ}, respectively. In the monolayer, the Λ\Lambda point in the BZ is defined as the valley occurring roughly half-way along the Γ−K\Gamma-K line (Fig. 1e). The 21.8∘21.8^{\circ} and 38.2∘38.2^{\circ} are mirror-symmetric and have the same size superlattice, but different proximity of the top and bottom layer valleys. In 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}, the bottom layer’s Λb\Lambda_{b} valley is closer to the top layer’s Λt\Lambda_{t} valley with the same spin, while in 38.2∘38.2^{\circ}, the Λb\Lambda_{b} valley is closer to the Λt′\Lambda^{\prime}_{t} valley with the opposite spin (Fig. 1b and c). We expect a large gap opening at the k-point where the Λ\Lambda valleys of the two layers intersect with the same spin.

Fig. 1d shows the path in the BZ used to compute the band structures.Fig. 1f displays the band structure computed using density functional theory (DFT) calculations with G​WGW (where G stands for the single-particle Green’s function and W is the screened Coulomb interaction) self-energy corrections [5] for both the 21.8∘ twisted WSe2 and the mirror-symmetric 38.2∘ structure. Along the path between the λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime} points, a flat band emerges only in the 21.8∘ superlattice driven by strong hybridization between the like-spin adjacent valleys of the two layers (Fig. 1b). On the other hand, in the 38.2∘ twisted bilayer, opposite spins in the adjacent valleys of the two layers (Fig. 1b) couple weakly, restoring a dispersive conduction band. In the 21.8∘ system, we also observe a second flat band emerge along the same path in the BZ at an energy separation of ∼\sim150 meV from the CBM. This is related to a similar coupling between the higher energy valleys at the Λ\Lambda point separated through spin-orbit coupling (see comparison to individual monolayers in SI Fig. S1). As expected, the valence and conduction band valleys at the κ\kappa point in the moiré BZ do not feature any renormalization due to the large twist angle. In 21.8∘, the VBM is two-fold degenerate and in 38.2∘, Umklapp scattering induces a small gap of 2.7 meV.

Fig. 2a visualizes the energy of the first unoccupied band in the moiré BZ for the 21.8° structure. The band has a strong anisotropy at the conduction band minimum, forming a flat band connecting the six λ\lambda points in the BZ. Moving away from this flat valley in a perpendicular direction causes the energy to rise sharply as displayed in Fig. 2b. We refer to this unique quasi-one-dimensional valley as a taco flat band (Fig. 2b). We note that this dispersion is fundamentally different from other well-known band structures such as the Mexican hat dispersion which features a central energy peak surrounded by an isotropic ring of low-energy states. Additionally, this dispersion is distinct because each segment connecting the adjacent λ\lambda valleys has a unique spin.

Alternating spin structure

To examine the spin texture of the 21.8∘ twisted bilayer WSe2, we computed the expectation value of the out-of-plane spin operator, ⟨Sz⟩\langle S_{z}\rangle, for each electronic state (more details in the supplementary information). Traversing the path connecting λ\lambda valleys in the moiré BZ (Fig. 3a), the spin character of the flat bands alternates (Fig. 3b). This unique spin texture is a direct signature of the underlying spin-selective interlayer hybridization and it represents a key feature of the taco flat band. The spin alternates for every 60° rotation, which is reminiscent of ff-wave altermagnetism [51]. The higher energy flat band, which is a result of spin-orbit coupling, has the opposite spin.

Evidence of magic angle at 21.8∘

To understand the electronic structure as one deviates from the 21.8∘ angle, we performed DFT calculations on six additional twisted WSe2 structures. The range of angles considered was between 13.17∘ to 27.8∘. We corrected the DFT band gap by a rigid shift to the GW band gap of natural bilayer WSe2. In Fig. 4b, we show the electronic band structure at 21.8∘. At this angle, the distance in momentum space between adjacent λ\lambda valleys is optimal such that the interlayer hybridization induces a flat band along the λ−λ′\lambda-\lambda^{\prime} path. Figures 4a and 4c illustrate the limiting cases. At 13.17∘13.17^{\circ}, which is a commensurate 19×19\sqrt{19}\times\sqrt{19} size superlattice, the smaller momentum difference between λ\lambda valleys reduces the energy at which the valleys cross and the hybridization leads to a dispersive band with a pronounced negative curvature. In contrast, at 27.8∘27.8^{\circ}, which is a commensurate 13×13\sqrt{13}\times\sqrt{13} size supercell, the larger valley separation leads to a dispersive band connecting the λ\lambda valleys with positive curvature. In Fig. 4d, we show the DOS for all of the structures considered. The DOS further highlights the unique behavior at 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}. Specifically, only at this angle does a vHS appear at the CBM. This vHS is a clear signature of the flat band formed between the λ\lambda valleys. Moving away from 21.8∘21.8^{\circ} broadens the peak and reduces its amplitude. An apparent ordering of the peaks is present according to the twist angle. This successive ordering is a direct result of how the twist angle tunes the band structure. The proximity of adjancent λ\lambda valleys at the 13.17∘ twist angle pushes the CBM to a lower energy, causing the DOS peak to appear first. At the 27.8∘ twist angle, the interlayer hybridization is weaker and thus the CBM relaxes to a higher energy leading to a DOS peak that appears last. The ”magic” angle, 21.8∘, represents an intermediate case. A second large DOS peak at higher energy in 21.8∘21.8^{\circ} arises from the second flat band, described above. Twist angles within ±0.5∘\pm 0.5^{\circ} of 21.8∘21.8^{\circ} require superlattice calculations with more than 55600 atoms and therefore prohibitively large for DFT calculations; instead, we construct a continuum model fitted to the DFT data to gain a richer understanding of the twist-angle dependence and quasi-1D physics of the taco flat band.

Magic angle near 21.8∘ in the low-energy model

We analyze the twist-angle dependence near 21.8∘ using a simplified low-energy model for the conduction bands (see Supplementary Information for details). By folding the Λ\Lambda valleys of the lowest conduction bands of the top and bottom layers into the moiré Brillouin zone (mBZ), we obtain a 12×1212\times 12 Hamiltonian that captures the relevant low-energy physics.

To describe the band flattening along the λ\lambda–λ′\lambda^{\prime} line, we focus on a 2×22\times 2 subblock of the full Hamiltonian describing a pair of adjacent λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime} valleys. Taking the midpoint of the λ\lambda–λ′\lambda^{\prime} line as the origin, the effective Hamiltonian reads

Because of the phenomenological moiré potential and the intrinsic anisotropy of the Λ\Lambda valleys, both rshiftr_{\textrm{shift}} and mm depend on θ\theta. However, the θ\theta-dependence of k0k_{0} alone already captures the essential features of the magic angle. We therefore first consider a simplified model where only k0k_{0} varies with θ\theta, keeping rshiftr_{\textrm{shift}} and mm fixed, and later compare it with full numerical results that include all θ\theta-dependent terms.

Owing to twofold rotational symmetry about the γ\gamma–κ\kappa (γ\gamma–κ′\kappa^{\prime}) axis and time-reversal symmetry, the tunneling term takes the form t⁡(k)≈ei​ϕo​(w0+ei​ϕr​w2​k2)t(k)\approx e^{i\phi_{o}}(w_{0}+e^{i\phi_{r}}w_{2}k^{2}), where ϕo\phi_{o} and ϕr\phi_{r} represent the overall and relative phases, respectively. The overall phase does not affect the energy spectrum E±​(k)=(k02​m+k2​m±2​k02​k2​m2+m4​|t⁡(k)|2)/2​m2E_{\pm}(k)=(k_{0}^{2}m+k^{2}m\pm 2\sqrt{k_{0}^{2}k^{2}m^{2}+m^{4}|t(k)|^{2}})/2m^{2}, where E−​(k)E_{-}(k) corresponds to the lowest conduction band dispersion. Fitting to first-principles results yields w0≈0.14175w_{0}\approx 0.14175 eV, w2≈0.49357​a02w_{2}\approx 0.49357~a_{0}^{2} eV, and ϕr≈1.105\phi_{r}\approx 1.105.

For small twist angles, the λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime} valleys strongly overlap and form a single minimum at k=0k=0, giving Δ​E1\Delta E_{1} as the bandwidth. As θ\theta increases, E−​(0)E_{-}(0) rises relative to E−​(k0)E_{-}(k_{0}), reducing Δ​E1\Delta E_{1}. Beyond a critical angle, the curvature at k=0k=0 changes sign, producing two symmetric minima between k=0k=0 and ±k0\pm k_{0}. Power-law dependence of the density of states

To confirm that the minimized bandwidth at the magic angle leads to the DOS peak observed in DFT calculations, we compute the DOS using the model Hamiltonian. Fig. 5d shows the calculated DOS for θ=18∘\theta=18^{\circ}, 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}, and 25∘25^{\circ}. A pronounced peak appears at the lower edge of the conduction band only at θ=21.8∘\theta=21.8^{\circ}, originating from the flattening of the taco band dispersion. Fig. 5e shows the log10⁡D⁡(Δ​E)\log_{10}D(\Delta E) vs. log10⁡Δ​E\log_{10}\Delta E plot for θ=21.8∘\theta=21.8^{\circ}, where Δ​E≡E−E−​(0)\Delta E\equiv E-E_{-}(0) and E−​(0)E_{-}(0) denotes the divergence energy. The log–log curve is linear in the range −3.5≲log10⁡Δ​E≲−2-3.5\lesssim\log_{10}\Delta E\lesssim-2 with slope ≈−0.205\approx-0.205, indicating that the DOS follows a power-law relation, D⁡(Δ​E)∝(Δ​E)−0.205D(\Delta E)\propto(\Delta E)^{-0.205}. The upper bound of this power-law regime corresponds to the width of the peak structure (∼10\sim 10 meV), whereas at higher energies the spectrum crosses over to approximately quadratic dispersion, yielding a constant DOS.

The power-law DOS originates from the effectively quasi-one-dimensional (1D) dispersion. To illustrate this, we consider the model dispersion

ε⁡(k)=a​kx2+b​ky2+c​ky4.\varepsilon(\textbf{k})=ak_{x}^{2}+bk_{y}^{2}+ck_{y}^{4}. (6)

Several limiting cases are instructive: (i) For a=b>0a=b>0, the dispersion describes a rotationally symmetric band minimum at kx=ky=0k_{x}=k_{y}=0, yielding a constant DOS proportional to the effective mass 1/(2​a)1/(2a). (ii) For aa and bb of opposite sign, the dispersion forms a saddle point, leading to the well-known vHS with logarithmic divergence at ε=0\varepsilon=0. (iii) For b=c=0b=c=0, the dispersion becomes perfectly 1D, where the DOS diverges as a power law with exponent −1/2-1/2. Our model produces a divergence with exponent −0.205-0.205, which is weaker than that of the ideal 1D case (iii). This can be understood by considering the case a>0a>0, c>0c>0, and b=0b=0: the dispersion still hosts a band minimum at the origin but is extremely flat along the yy-direction within a finite momentum window, giving D(ΔE)∝(ΔE)−1/4D(\Delta E)\propto(\Delta E)^{-1/4}.

Because |b|≪a,c|b|\ll a,c, the system behaves approximately as in the quadratic–quartic case, yielding an effective power-law DOS with an exponent slightly smaller than −1/4-1/4. However, since b<0b<0 while a>0a>0, the band also hosts a van Hove singularity that produces a logarithmic divergence at very low energies. The lower bound of the power-law regime in Fig. 5e reflects this crossover: for energies above the taco-band bandwidth (∼1\sim 1 meV), the log–log DOS plot shows a clear linear trend consistent with the power-law scaling, whereas for Δ​E<10−3.5\Delta E<10^{-3.5} eV (∼0.3\sim 0.3 meV) the curve deviates from linearity, signaling the reemergence of the underlying logarithmic divergence associated with the van Hove singularity.

This analysis, purely based on energy bands, may significantly change at low electron fillings, where the Coulomb interaction generally dominates over the kinetic energy. The quasi-1D character is thus expected to emerge only at intermediate fillings, neither too small nor too large. Estimating the interaction scale as U≈14.4/(ϵ​d)U\approx 14.4/(\epsilon d) eV, where d=7​a0/n∼8.7/nd=\sqrt{7}a_{0}/n\sim 8.7/n Å is the mean electron separation per moiré unit cell and ϵ=6.24\epsilon=6.24 for WSe2 [22], we obtain the filling-dependent interaction strength shown as a blue curve in Fig. 5f. When the Fermi energy is below about 1.5 meV, UU exceeds 40 times the Fermi energy, potentially leading to Wigner crystallization [63, 54, 17, 43], indicating a strongly correlated regime that can obscure the van Hove singularity. However, there exists an intermediate Fermi-energy window of the quasi-1D character before the interaction strength falls below the Wigner-crystal threshold. In this regime, the enhanced DOS and strong Fermi-surface nesting associated with the taco band favor band-structure-driven instabilities. Including realistic gate screening further suppresses the Coulomb energy [magenta curve in Fig. 5f], enlarging this window and making the underlying van Hove singularity and quasi-1D features more prominent.

Discussion

Our work reveals that twisted bilayer WSe2 at θ=21.8∘\theta=21.8^{\circ} has an intriguing electronic structure termed taco bands, which uniquely combines three intriguing band properties: quasi-one-dimensional dispersion, concentric Fermi surfaces, and momentum-dependent spin polarization. We further demonstrate that this phenomenon is generic across twisted TMDs. Our analysis of three additional twisted bilayer TMDs shows that WS2 likewise exhibits flat bands at 21.8∘, while MoSe2 and MoS2 have a different magic angle that is slightly larger than 21.8∘ (see details in SI Fig. S2).

Quasi-one-dimensional behavior usually arises from chain-like atomic bonding in real space, and manifests as approximately parallel Fermi surfaces extended across the two-dimensional BZ [21, 59, 60, 28, 18, 67, 15, 33]. In such systems, low-energy excitations can show Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL) behavior in a finite temperature range [56, 41]. On the other hand, concentric Fermi surfaces emerge from Mexican-hat-type [62, 50, 27, 26] or Rashba spin–orbit-coupled dispersions [4, 24], where the local band minima form a ringlike shape such that Fermi surfaces are annular. Since their band structure is locally quasi-one-dimensional, correlation effects are strongly enhanced [14, 20]. However, TLL behavior is incompatible with an annular Fermi surface, where the radial (dispersive) and angular (dispersionless) directions are globally entangled around the ring. The taco bands reconciles these limits: hexagonally concentric Fermi surfaces that contain extended quasi-one-dimensional segments. This geometry allows TLL-like responses to emerge on finite arcs while preserving a global concentric shape, enabling an intriguing interplay between 1D and 2D physics. Moreover, each quasi-one-dimensional valley is strongly spin-polarized, resulting in alternating spin-up and spin-down texture in momentum space, similar to that in altermagnetic MnTe [51, 30, 29]. In conclusion, the combination of pronounced one-dimensional character, concentric Fermi surfaces, and alternating spin texture in twisted WSe2 provides a novel platform to probe interaction-driven instabilities.

Methods

S0.1 First-principles calculations

Density functional theory calculations: Moiré structures were generated using the Twister[9] code. Structural relaxations were completed using classical force field calculations with LAMMPS [14, 11], employing the Stillinger Weber [13] potential for intralayer interactions and the Kolmogorov-Crespi potential [8] for interlayer coupling. The relaxed configurations served as input for electronic structure calculations that were performed using the strictly localized atomic orbitals DFT framework implemented in the SIESTA[12, 4] package. The generalized gradient approximation (GGA) in the Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE)[10] implementation was employed for the exchange-correlation functional. Fully relativistic norm-conserving pseudopotentials were used in the DFT calculations. For the DFT calculations, the real space grid to represent physical quantities was constrained to a cutoff of 160 Ry. For the structures twisted at 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}, the BZ was sampled using a 30x30x1 k - point grid without symmetry reduction. To sample the BZ of the other structures considered, the number of k - points was scaled in accordance to the moiré wavelength relative to the period at 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}. The DOS was subsequently computed and normalized per atom using a Gaussian smearing method according to the formula: g(E) = 1 N atoms 1 N k ∑_n, k 1 σ π exp(-( E - (E n, k - E F ) σ )^2) where NatomsN_{\text{atoms}} is the number of atoms in the supercell and NkN_{k} is the total number of k-points. The sum runs over all band indices nn and k-points 𝐤\mathbf{k}. The term En,𝐤−EFE_{n,\mathbf{k}}-E_{F} represents the eigenvalues relative to the Fermi level, and σ\sigma is the Gaussian broadening width, which was set to 0.009 eV. This yields a DOS with units of states per eV per atom.

GW calculations: We computed the quasiparticle band gap correction for the twisted bilayer WSe2 structures using single-shot G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations [5], performed with the BerkeleyGW package [3]. These calculations were conducted on an AB-stacked unit cell whose interlayer spacing was set to match that of the twisted bilayers, thereby ensuring a similar screening environment. The dielectric matrix was constructed within the random-phase approximation (RPA) with a 30 Ry cutoff and 5109 unoccupied bands. We sampled the Brillouin-zone using a 12×12×1 k-mesh, accelerating convergence with the non-uniform neck sub-sampling method [2].

Spin texture: The spin texture of the 21.8∘21.8^{\circ} t–WSe2 moiré superlattice was obtained from fully relativistic, non-collinear DFT calculations. At every band index nn and crystal momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k} we solved the Kohn–Sham equation for a two-component spinor

Ψn​𝐤​(𝐫)=(ψn​𝐤↑​(𝐫)ψn​𝐤↓​(𝐫)),\Psi_{n\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,\uparrow}(\mathbf{r})\\[4.0pt] \psi_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,\downarrow}(\mathbf{r})\end{pmatrix},

whose upper and lower components give the probability amplitudes for finding the electron at position 𝐫\mathbf{r} with spin projection ↑\uparrow or ↓\downarrow along the global zz axis, respectively. Each component is expanded in a plane-wave basis,

ψn​𝐤s(𝐫)=∑𝐆cn​𝐤s(𝐆)ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)⋅𝐫,s∈{↑,↓},\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,s}(\mathbf{r})\;=\;\sum_{\mathbf{G}}c_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,s}(\mathbf{G})\;e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}},\qquad s\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\},

where 𝐆=h​𝐛1+k​𝐛2+ℓ​𝐛3\mathbf{G}=h\,\mathbf{b}_{1}+k\,\mathbf{b}_{2}+\ell\,\mathbf{b}_{3} is a reciprocal-lattice vector of the moiré supercell (h,k,ℓ∈ℤh,k,\ell\in\mathbb{Z}; 𝐛i\mathbf{b}_{i} are its primitive reciprocal vectors), cn​𝐤s​(𝐆)∈ℂc_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,s}(\mathbf{G})\in\mathbb{C} is the plane-wave coefficient. The spin-resolved norm of a state is therefore ∥ψn​𝐤s∥2=∑𝐆|cn​𝐤s​(𝐆)|2\lVert\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,s}\rVert^{2}=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}|c_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,s}(\mathbf{G})|^{2}, and the expectation value of the Pauli operator σz\sigma_{z} is

⟨Sz⟩n​𝐤=ℏ2​(∥ψn​𝐤↑∥2−∥ψn​𝐤↓∥2)=ℏ2​(∑𝐆|cn​𝐤↑​(𝐆)|2−∑𝐆|cn​𝐤↓​(𝐆)|2).\bigl\langle S_{z}\bigr\rangle_{n\mathbf{k}}=\frac{\hbar}{2}\!\left(\lVert\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,\uparrow}\rVert^{2}-\lVert\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,\downarrow}\rVert^{2}\right)=\frac{\hbar}{2}\!\left(\sum_{\mathbf{G}}|c_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,\uparrow}(\mathbf{G})|^{2}-\sum_{\mathbf{G}}|c_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\,\downarrow}(\mathbf{G})|^{2}\right).

To visualize this spin texture in the band structure plot, for each band, the color of each line segment (k-point) is determined by its corresponding ⟨Sz⟩\langle S_{z}\rangle value. A custom colormap was used, mapping positive spin polarization (spin-up) to red and negative polarization (spin-down) to blue. States with a near-zero spin polarization, where the bands are effectively degenerate, are colored grey.

S0.2 Moiré band model

In this section, we construct a continuum model that describes the band flattening along the λ−λ′\lambda-\lambda^{\prime} direction in twisted bilayer WSe2 around a specific commensurate twist angle of 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}, where λ\lambda (λ′\lambda^{\prime}) denotes the band minimum of the γ−κ\gamma-\kappa (γ−κ′\gamma-\kappa^{\prime}) line. Here, γ=(0,0)\gamma=(0,0), κ=a0−1sin(θ/2)(−43π/3,4π/3)\kappa=a_{0}^{-1}\sin(\theta/2)(-4\sqrt{3}\pi/3,4\pi/3) and κ′=a0−1sin(θ/2)(−43π/3,−4π/3)\kappa^{\prime}=a_{0}^{-1}\sin(\theta/2)(-4\sqrt{3}\pi/3,-4\pi/3) represent high-symmetry points of the moiré Brillouin zone (mBZ). a0a_{0} is the lattice constant of monolayer WSe2. We use lowercase Greek letters to denote points in the mBZ to distinguish them from those of the top and bottom monolayers.

Monolayer WSe2 tight-binding model— We adopted the Hamiltonian and parameters from Ref. [6] for the tungsten dd-orbital tight-binding model without spin-orbit coupling in the basis of (dz2,dx​y,dx2−y2d_{z^{2}},d_{xy},d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}).

Fig. S3 shows the band structure obtained from this tight-binding model. Without doping, only the bottom band is occupied. Our main interest is on the minima of the lowest unoccupied band located close to the midpoints of the Γ−K\Gamma-K and Γ−K′\Gamma-K^{\prime} lines. We refer to these band minima as the Λ\Lambda valleys, and we denote the corresponding midpoint momenta as the QQ points. Within the first Brillouin zone (BZ), there are six inequivalent QQ points. We denote them as QiQ_{i} with i=1,2,⋯,6i=1,2,\cdots,6, where

Q1=a0−1​(2​π/3,0).Q_{1}=a_{0}^{-1}(2\pi/3,0). (S1)

The actual minimum on the Γ−K\Gamma-K line, Λ1=a0−1​(2.0975,0)\Lambda_{1}=a_{0}^{-1}(2.0975,0), is very close to Q1≈a0−1​(2.0944,0)Q_{1}\approx a_{0}^{-1}(2.0944,0). The other QQ points are generated by successive 60∘ rotations, i.e.

Qi=[R⁡(π/3)](i−1)​Q1,Q_{i}=[R(\pi/3)]^{(i-1)}Q_{1}, (S2)

where R⁡(ϕ)=(cos⁡ϕ−sin⁡ϕsin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ)R(\phi)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\phi&-\sin\phi\\ \sin\phi&\cos\phi\end{pmatrix} is a rotation matrix. The energy dispersion near QiQ_{i} is quadratic. The effective mass of the Λ1\Lambda_{1} valley is

mx\displaystyle m_{x} ≈0.849/(a02​eV),\displaystyle\approx 0.849/(a_{0}^{2}~\textrm{eV}), (S3)
my\displaystyle m_{y} ≈0.749/(a02​eV),\displaystyle\approx 0.749/(a_{0}^{2}~\textrm{eV}), (S4)

in the kxk_{x} and kyk_{y} directions, respectively.

After twisting, the Q1Q_{1} point of the bottom and top layers, denoted as Q1​bQ_{1b} and Q1​tQ_{1t}, are folded to the q1q_{1} and q2q_{2} points which are the midpoints of the γ−κ\gamma-\kappa and γ−κ′\gamma-\kappa^{\prime} lines in the mBZ, as shown in Fig. S4a. Here,

q1=a0−1​2​π​sin⁡θ2​(13,13),q_{1}=a_{0}^{-1}2\pi\sin\frac{\theta}{2}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{1}{3}), (S5)

and

qi=[R⁡(π/3)](i−1)​q1.q_{i}=[R(\pi/3)]^{(i-1)}q_{1}. (S6)

While we are interested in the region close to these points, the actual band minima λi\lambda_{i}s of twisted bilayer WSe2 at the twist angle 21.8∘21.8^{\circ} are not located at qiq_{i}s. As our first-principles calculations show, the distance between λi\lambda_{i} and qiq_{i} is greatly amplified by twisting, compared to the original small deviation between Λi\Lambda_{i} and QiQ_{i}. Although both λi\lambda_{i} and qiq_{i} lie along the γ−κ\gamma-\kappa or γ−κ′\gamma-\kappa^{\prime} line, the distance from γ\gamma to λi\lambda_{i} is about 0.7 times that from γ\gamma to qiq_{i}. This significant shift is due to the moiré potential that applies to each valley. We discuss this effect in detail later in the section moiré potential.

Upon including spin–orbit coupling in the model, the band near the Λ\Lambda valleys splits into two almost spin-polarized branches separated by approximately 0.240.24 eV [7]. Importantly, between these two spin branches, the spin-up band has lower energy at the Λi\Lambda_{i} valleys with odd ii, whereas the spin-down band lies lower at the Λi\Lambda_{i} valleys with even ii, reflecting the alternating sign of the spin–orbit coupling along the Γ−K\Gamma-K versus Γ−K′\Gamma-K^{\prime} directions.

In the following, we construct a spin-polarized continuum model of twisted WSe2, based on the quadratic kinetic-energy dispersion (kx−[kQi]x)2/(2​mx)+(ky−[kQi]y)2/(2​my)(k_{x}-[\textbf{k}_{Q_{i}}]_{x})^{2}/(2m_{x})+(k_{y}-[\textbf{k}_{Q_{i}}]_{y})^{2}/(2m_{y}) at the QiQ_{i} valleys of monolayer WSe2. We show that the partially flat band—dispersionless along one direction but dispersive along the other—which we refer to as the taco band, arises from interlayer tunneling that opens a gap between bands from two nearby valleys. Since the valley momenta lie on the γ−κ\gamma-\kappa or γ−κ′\gamma-\kappa^{\prime} lines, the band flattening appears along the lines connecting these valleys. Consequently, the taco band emerges along the edges of the hexagon formed by the six λi\lambda_{i} points.

Continuum model Hamiltonian of twisted WSe2— The Hamiltonian operator is in the form of

H^=∑k,k′(ψt,k†,ψb,k′†)​H​(k,k′)​(ψt,k,ψb,k′)T,\hat{H}=\sum_{\textbf{k},\textbf{k}^{\prime}}(\psi_{t,\textbf{k}}^{\dagger},\psi_{b,\textbf{k}^{\prime}}^{\dagger})H(\textbf{k},\textbf{k}^{\prime})(\psi_{t,\textbf{k}},\psi_{b,\textbf{k}^{\prime}})^{T}, (S7)

where ψl,n,k†\psi_{l,n,\textbf{k}}^{\dagger} (ψl,n,k\psi_{l,n,\textbf{k}}) is the creation (annihilation) operator of an electron in a Bloch state with the layer index l=t,bl=t,b, valley index nn, and momentum k. The indices with and without a prime sign denote that the Bloch state is from the bottom and top layer, respectively. In momentum space, the valleys form a reciprocal lattice with periodicity

gi=[R(+θ/2)−R(−θ/2)]Gi\textbf{g}_{i}=[R(+\theta/2)-R(-\theta/2)]\textbf{G}_{i} (S8)

for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, where G1=a0−1​(0,4​π/3)\textbf{G}_{1}=a_{0}^{-1}(0,4\pi/\sqrt{3}) and Gi=[R⁡(2​π/3)](i−1)​G1\textbf{G}_{i}=[R(2\pi/3)]^{(i-1)}\textbf{G}_{1}. Thus, as in Fig. S5, the valley center in momentum space satisfies kn=kqi+z1​(n)​g1+z2​(n)​g2\textbf{k}_{n}=\textbf{k}_{q_{i}}+z_{1}(n)\textbf{g}_{1}+z_{2}(n)\textbf{g}_{2} where z1​(n)z_{1}(n) and z2​(n)z_{2}(n) are integers.

In the Bloch state basis, diagonal elements of H⁡(k,k′)H(\textbf{k},\textbf{k}^{\prime}) take the form

Ht,n​n​(k)\displaystyle H_{t,nn}(\textbf{k}) ≡[H⁡(k,k′)]t,n;t,n=⟨t,n,k​|H^|​t,n,k⟩=(k−kn)22​m+Δn​(k),\displaystyle\equiv[H(\textbf{k},\textbf{k}^{\prime})]_{t,n;t,n}=\langle t,n,\textbf{k}|\hat{H}|t,n,\textbf{k}\rangle=\frac{(\textbf{k}-\textbf{k}_{n})^{2}}{2m}+\Delta_{n}(\textbf{k}), (S9)
Hb,n′​n′​(k′)\displaystyle H_{b,n^{\prime}n^{\prime}}(\textbf{k}^{\prime}) ≡[H⁡(k,k′)]b,n′;b,n′=⟨b,n′,k′​|H^|​b,n′,k′⟩=(k′−kn′)22​m+Δn′​(k′),\displaystyle\equiv[H(\textbf{k},\textbf{k}^{\prime})]_{b,n^{\prime};b,n^{\prime}}=\langle b,n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}|\hat{H}|b,n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}\rangle=\frac{(\textbf{k}^{\prime}-\textbf{k}^{\prime}_{n})^{2}}{2m}+\Delta_{n^{\prime}}(\textbf{k}^{\prime}), (S10)

where |l,n,k⟩=ψl,n,k†|0⟩|l,n,\textbf{k}\rangle=\psi_{l,n,\textbf{k}}^{\dagger}|0\rangle, mm is the effective mass of an electron near the valleys, and Δn​(k)\Delta_{n}(\textbf{k}) represents the moiré potential. Meanwhile, the off-diagonal elements of [H⁡(k,k′)]t,n;b,n′[H(\textbf{k},\textbf{k}^{\prime})]_{t,n;b,n^{\prime}} describe the interlayer tunneling ΔT​(n,k,n′,k′)\Delta_{T}(n,\textbf{k};n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}) between two Bloch states |t,n,k⟩|t,n,\textbf{k}\rangle and |b,n′,k′⟩|b,n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}\rangle.

Moiré potential— Δn​(k)\Delta_{n}(\textbf{k}) is a phenomenological term that incorporates all effects of the other layer, except for the direct tunneling between two valleys, which is included in ΔT​(n,k,n′,k′)\Delta_{T}(n,\textbf{k};n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}). Δn​(k)\Delta_{n}(\textbf{k}) is periodic in the mBZ and can therefore be expanded in a Fourier series of moiré reciprocal lattice vectors. For simplicity, we retain the leading harmonic term, which takes the form cos⁡(a⋅k+φ)\cos{(\textbf{a}\cdot\textbf{k}+\varphi)}, where a is a moiré lattice vector and φ\varphi is a constant phase. We note that non-zero φ\varphi is allowed in Δn​(k)\Delta_{n}(\textbf{k}) even though the full system has time-reversal symmetry, because we are currently looking at only one spin sector of the Hamiltonian. In the full Hamiltonian, Δqi​(k)\Delta_{q_{i}}(\textbf{k}) is symmetry-related to another Δqj​(k)\Delta_{q_{j}}(\textbf{k}) with opposite spin by time-reversal, but Δn​(k)\Delta_{n}(\textbf{k}) itself is not required to be an even function of k. Imposing the three-fold rotational symmetry around the zz-axis (C3​zC_{3z}), we have

Δn=A​cos⁡(an⋅k+φ),\Delta_{n}=A\cos{(\textbf{a}_{n}\cdot\textbf{k}+\varphi)}, (S11)

where AA is the amplitude of the moiré potential and an\textbf{a}_{n} is a moiré lattice vector that is parallel to kn\textbf{k}_{n} valleys inside the first mBZ. For example, for the q1q_{1} and q2q_{2} valleys in Fig. S4, the corresponding moiré lattice vectors are aq1,q2=a0(1/sin(θ/2))(−3/4,±1/4)\textbf{a}_{q_{1},q_{2}}=a_{0}(1/\sin{(\theta/2)})(-\sqrt{3}/4,\pm 1/4). Fitting the DFT data, we obtain

A\displaystyle A =−0.12115​eV,\displaystyle=-0.12115~\textrm{eV}, (S12)
φ\displaystyle\varphi =0.5.\displaystyle=0.5. (S13)

As shown in Fig. S6, the effect of the moiré potential in our model is to shift the band minima from the qiq_{i} valleys to the λi\lambda_{i} valleys. The parameters AA and φ\varphi are determined by fitting to the first-principles results at 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}.

Interlayer tunneling— ΔT​(n,k,n′,k′)\Delta_{T}(n,\textbf{k};n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}) is obtained using the two-center approximation [1]. The hopping integral between two Bloch states |n,k⟩|n,\textbf{k}\rangle and |n′,k′⟩|n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}\rangle is given by

ΔT​(n,k,n′,k′)\displaystyle\Delta_{T}(n,\textbf{k};n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}) ≡⟨t,n,k​|H^|​b,n′,k′⟩\displaystyle\equiv\langle t,n,\textbf{k}|\hat{H}|b,n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}\rangle (S14)
=∑R,R′ei​k′⋅R′−i​k⋅RN​N′​⟨t,n,R​|H^|​b,n′,R′⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\textbf{R},\textbf{R}^{\prime}}\frac{e^{i\textbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\textbf{R}^{\prime}-i\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{R}}}{\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}}\langle t,n,\textbf{R}|\hat{H}|b,n^{\prime},\textbf{R}^{\prime}\rangle
=∑R,R′ei​k′⋅R′−i​k⋅RN​N′​tn​n′​(R′−R)\displaystyle=\sum_{\textbf{R},\textbf{R}^{\prime}}\frac{e^{i\textbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\textbf{R}^{\prime}-i\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{R}}}{\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}}t_{nn^{\prime}}(\textbf{R}^{\prime}-\textbf{R})
=∑R,R′ei​k′⋅R′−i​k⋅RN​N′∑qe−iq⋅(R′−R)tn​n′(q)\displaystyle=\sum_{\textbf{R},\textbf{R}^{\prime}}\frac{e^{i\textbf{k}^{\prime}\cdot\textbf{R}^{\prime}-i\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{R}}}{NN^{\prime}}\sum_{\textbf{q}}e^{-i\textbf{q}\cdot(\textbf{R}^{\prime}-\textbf{R})}t_{nn^{\prime}}(\textbf{q})
=∑qtn​n′​(q)​∑R,R′ei⁡(k′−q)⋅R′−i⁡(k−q)⋅RN​N′\displaystyle=\sum_{\textbf{q}}t_{nn^{\prime}}(\textbf{q})\sum_{\textbf{R},\textbf{R}^{\prime}}\frac{e^{i(\textbf{k}^{\prime}-\textbf{q})\cdot\textbf{R}^{\prime}-i(\textbf{k}-\textbf{q})\cdot\textbf{R}}}{NN^{\prime}}
=∑qtn​n′(q)∑G,G′δk−q,Gδk′−q,G′e−iG⋅d\displaystyle=\sum_{\textbf{q}}t_{nn^{\prime}}(\textbf{q})\sum_{\textbf{G},\textbf{G}^{\prime}}\delta_{\textbf{k}-\textbf{q},\textbf{G}}\delta_{\textbf{k}^{\prime}-\textbf{q},\textbf{G}^{\prime}}e^{-i\textbf{G}\cdot\textbf{d}}
=∑G,G′δk+G,k′+G′​tn​n′​(k+G)​ei​G⋅d,\displaystyle=\sum_{\textbf{G},\textbf{G}^{\prime}}\delta_{\textbf{k}+\textbf{G},\textbf{k}^{\prime}+\textbf{G}^{\prime}}t_{nn^{\prime}}(\textbf{k}+\textbf{G})e^{i\textbf{G}\cdot\textbf{d}},

where NN and N′N^{\prime} are the numbers of unit cells in the respective layers, and |n,R⟩|n,\textbf{R}\rangle and |n′,R′⟩|n^{\prime},\textbf{R}^{\prime}\rangle represent the Wannier states localized at R=j1​a1+j2​a2−d\textbf{R}=j_{1}\textbf{a}_{1}+j_{2}\textbf{a}_{2}-\textbf{d} and R′=j1′​a1′+j2′​a2′\textbf{R}^{\prime}=j^{\prime}_{1}\textbf{a}^{\prime}_{1}+j^{\prime}_{2}\textbf{a}^{\prime}_{2}, respectively. For i=1,2i=1,2, jij_{i} and ji′j^{\prime}_{i} are arbitrary integers, and ai\textbf{a}_{i} and ai′\textbf{a}^{\prime}_{i} are basis lattice vectors of the corresponding layers. d denotes the lateral displacement between the two layers.

Equation (S14) implies that for a given k, only k′\textbf{k}^{\prime} that satisfy k+G=k′+G′\textbf{k}+\textbf{G}=\textbf{k}^{\prime}+\textbf{G}^{\prime} yields non-zero value for the interlayer tunneling. Thus, for a Bloch state from the Q1​bQ_{1b} valley, Assuming that tn​n′​(R′−R)t_{nn^{\prime}}(\textbf{R}^{\prime}-\textbf{R}) decays exponentially with the distance |R′−R||\textbf{R}^{\prime}-\textbf{R}|, its Fourier transform tn​n′​(q)t_{nn^{\prime}}(\textbf{q}) also decays exponentially with |q||\textbf{q}|. Therefore, we consider only a few ⟨t,n,k​|H^|​b,n′,k′⟩\langle t,n,\textbf{k}|\hat{H}|b,n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime}\rangle with smallest values of k+G\textbf{k}+\textbf{G}, while truncating out larger G cases. In particular, at a momentum near the QiQ_{i} (Qi′Q^{\prime}_{i}) valleys, G=0\textbf{G}=0 is the only one for which k+G\textbf{k}+\textbf{G} lies within the first BZ. Hence, G=0\textbf{G}=0 yields the dominant contribution, and we obtain ΔT​(n,k,n′,k′)=tn​n′​(k)\Delta_{T}(n,\textbf{k};n^{\prime},\textbf{k}^{\prime})=t_{nn^{\prime}}(\textbf{k}) for k′\textbf{k}^{\prime}s such that k′=k−G′\textbf{k}^{\prime}=\textbf{k}-\textbf{G}^{\prime}. Since the Bloch states with k′\textbf{k}^{\prime}s for large G′\textbf{G}^{\prime}s have very high energies when they are folded back into the first mBZ, we only consider G=G′=0\textbf{G}=\textbf{G}^{\prime}=0 cases in our model. For example, from the lowest unoccupied states (which are the spin-up states) at Q1​bQ_{1b} and Q1​tQ_{1t} valleys in rotated monolayer WSe2 BZs, we obtain the following Hamiltonian for the q1q_{1} and q2q_{2} valleys in mBZ:

H↑​(k)=\displaystyle H_{\uparrow}(\textbf{k})=
(∑α=x,y[R(−θ/2)(k−kq1)]α22​mα​2​my+A​cos⁡(aq1⋅k+φ)t12​(k)t12∗​(k)∑α=x,y[R⁡(θ/2)​(k−kq2)]α22​mα+A​cos⁡(aq2⋅k+φ)).\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\sum_{\alpha=x,y}\frac{[R(-\theta/2)(\textbf{k}-\textbf{k}_{q_{1}})]_{\alpha}^{2}}{2m_{\alpha}}{2m_{y}}+A\cos{(\textbf{a}_{q_{1}}\cdot\textbf{k}+\varphi)}&t_{12}(\textbf{k})\\ t_{12}^{*}(\textbf{k})&\sum_{\alpha=x,y}\frac{[R(\theta/2)(\textbf{k}-\textbf{k}_{q_{2}})]_{\alpha}^{2}}{2m_{\alpha}}+A\cos{(\textbf{a}_{q_{2}}\cdot\textbf{k}+\varphi)}\end{pmatrix}. (S15)

S0.3 Low-energy band structure along λ−λ′\lambda-\lambda^{\prime}

In this section, we provide a detailed analysis of the low-energy band structure along the λ−λ′\lambda-\lambda^{\prime} direction, complementing the results discussed in the section Magic angle near 21.8∘ in the low-energy model of the main text.

Model Hamiltonian— Along the λ1−λ2\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2} line where kxk_{x} is fixed, the Hamiltonian in Eq. (S15) can be expressed as a function of kyk_{y} in a simpler form:

H↑​(ky)=((ky−k0​y)22​mt⁡(ky)t∗​(ky)(ky+k0​y)22​m),H_{\uparrow}(k_{y})=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{(k_{y}-k_{0y})^{2}}{2m}&t(k_{y})\\ t^{*}(k_{y})&\frac{(k_{y}+k_{0y})^{2}}{2m}\end{pmatrix}, (S16)

where k0​y≈0.700×(2​π/3)​sin⁡(θ/2)k_{0y}\approx 0.700\times(2\pi/3)\sin(\theta/2) a0−1a_{0}^{-1} with a0a_{0} denoting the lattice constant of monolayer WSe2. m≈0.80177​a0−2m\approx 0.80177~a_{0}^{-2} eV-1 is the effective mass along the λ1−λ2\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2} direction, obtained by taking the inverse of second derivative of diagonal elements in Eq. (S15).

Symmetry constraints of the effective Hamiltonian— Twisted bilayer WSe2 has time-reversal TT symmetry, three-fold rotation C3​zC_{3z} symmetry around the zz-axis, and two-fold rotation symmetries around three different in-plane axes which are related to each other by C3​zC_{3z}. In our calculation, one of the in-plane axis is taken to be the yy-axis, so we denote the twofold rotation as C2​yC_{2y}, C3​z​C2​y​C3​z−1C_{3z}C_{2y}C_{3z}^{-1}, and C3​z2​C2​y​C3​z−2C_{3z}^{2}C_{2y}C_{3z}^{-2}. The effective Hamiltonian in Eq. (S16) , which involves only two nearby valleys λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime} with the same spin, is not invariant under TT, C3​zC_{3z} and C2​yC_{2y} individually. However, the line connecting λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime} is invariant under C2​y​TC_{2y}T, the combination of TT and C2​yC_{2y}. The representation of C2​y​TC_{2y}T is given by (0110)​𝒦\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}\mathcal{K} where 𝒦\mathcal{K} is complex conjugation. Since H⁡(ky)H(k_{y}) satisfy (C2​y​T)​H​(ky)​(C2​y​T)−1=H⁡(−ky)(C_{2y}T)H(k_{y})(C_{2y}T)^{-1}=H(-k_{y}), we find that t⁡(ky)=t⁡(−ky)t(k_{y})=t(-k_{y}). Thus, in the lowest orders of kyk_{y},

t⁡(ky)≈w~0+w~2​ky2,t(k_{y})\approx\tilde{w}_{0}+\tilde{w}_{2}k_{y}^{2}, (S17)

where both w~0\tilde{w}_{0} and w~2\tilde{w}_{2} are complex numbers.

Fitted parameters— The eigenvalues of Eq. (S16) are given by

E±​(ky)=k0​y2​m+ky2​m±2​k0​y2​ky2​m2+m4​|t⁡(ky)|22​m2+E0,E_{\pm}(k_{y})=\frac{k_{0y}^{2}m+k_{y}^{2}m\pm 2\sqrt{k_{0y}^{2}k_{y}^{2}m^{2}+m^{4}|t(k_{y})|^{2}}}{2m^{2}}+E_{0}, (S18)

where E0E_{0} is an additional constant energy shift introduced to match the conduction band energy level obtained from first-principles calculations at ky=0k_{y}=0. We rewrite w~0=ei​ϕo​w0\tilde{w}_{0}=e^{i\phi_{o}}w_{0} and w~2=ei​ϕo​ei​ϕr​w2\tilde{w}_{2}=e^{i\phi_{o}}e^{i\phi_{r}}w_{2}, in which ϕo\phi_{o} and ϕr\phi_{r} represent the overall and relative phases of w~0\tilde{w}_{0} and w~2\tilde{w}_{2}, respectively. Then |t(ky)|2=w02+2w0w2ky2cosϕr+(w2ky2)2|t(k_{y})|^{2}=w_{0}^{2}+2w_{0}w_{2}k_{y}^{2}\cos{\phi_{r}}+(w_{2}k_{y}^{2})^{2}. Since only the relative phase ϕr\phi_{r} enters the expression for E±​(ky)E_{\pm}(k_{y}), the overall phase ϕo\phi_{o} does not affect the band dispersion and cannot be determined from it. We determine the model parameters by fitting the energy dispersion to the results from first-principles calculations. The value of w0w_{0} can be directly extracted from the relation E+​(0)−E−​(0)=2​w0E_{+}(0)-E_{-}(0)=2w_{0}, giving

w0≈0.14175​ eV.\displaystyle w_{0}\approx 0.14175\text{ eV}. (S19)

Fig. S7 shows the fitting results. With fitted parameters

w2\displaystyle w_{2} ≈0.49357​a02​ eV,\displaystyle\approx 0.49357~a_{0}^{2}\text{ eV}, (S20)
ϕr\displaystyle\phi_{r} ≈1.10536,\displaystyle\approx 1.10536, (S21)

the model almost perfectly reproduces the dispersion of the lower (flat) band and accurately captures the upper band’s behavior near ky=0k_{y}=0.

Bandwidth and magic angle— Using the same parameter values for mm, w0w_{0}, w2w_{2}, and ϕr\phi_{r}, we compute the band dispersion for different twist angles θ\theta. As expected, for a small twist angle (e.g., θ=18∘\theta=18^{\circ}), the dispersion of the lower band is convex downward, indicating that the two valleys are close in momentum space and the interlayer tunneling dominates, pushing bands downward at the midpoint of λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime}. In contrast, for a large twist angle (e.g., θ=25∘\theta=25^{\circ}), the dispersion becomes convex upward. This is because the two valleys are far apart, and the kinetic energy of electrons within each valley becomes the dominant contribution. At a specific intermediate twist angle, however, these two competing effects balance each other, resulting in an extremely flat band.

As illustrated in the main text, the bandwidth along the λ−λ′\lambda-\lambda^{\prime} line is given by the largest among the three energy differences:

Δ​E1\displaystyle\Delta E_{1} =|E−​(0)−E−​(k0​y)|,\displaystyle=|E_{-}(0)-E_{-}(k_{0y})|, (S22)

where EminE_{\textrm{min}} denotes the minimum—if present—of E−​(ky)E_{-}(k_{y}) between ky=0k_{y}=0 and ky=k0​yk_{y}=k_{0y} (See Fig. S8). The minima appear at

While the twist-angle dependence was encoded only in k0​yk_{0y} in our analysis above, other quantities—such as the effective mass along the λ−λ′\lambda-\lambda^{\prime} direction and the band minima shift along the γ−κ\gamma-\kappa (γ−κ′\gamma-\kappa^{\prime}) direction—are in fact also θ\theta-dependent. This is because, as shown in Eq. (S15), θ\theta enters the diagonal elements of the Hamiltonian explicitly through R(±θ/2)R(\pm\theta/2), aq1\textbf{a}_{q_{1}}, and aq2\textbf{a}_{q_{2}}. Keeping only w0w_{0}, w2w_{2}, and ϕr\phi_{r} fixed, we compute the dispersions for twist angles near 21.8∘21.8^{\circ} [Fig. S9] and compare the numerically obtained Δ​E1\Delta E_{1} with the analytic result. As shown in Fig 5c of the main text, the discrepancy between the analytic approximation and the numerical calculation increases as θ\theta deviates from the reference angle of 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}. Nevertheless, Δ​E1\Delta E_{1} remains a reliable indicator of the bandwidth, and the magic angle is still found to lie very close to 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}. From the numerical analysis that considers the twist-angle dependence of the effective mass and band minima shift, the magic twist angle corresponding to the minimum bandwidth is found to be θc,num=21.7∘\theta_{c,\text{num}}=21.7^{\circ}.

The magic angle discussed above corresponds to the twist angle that minimizes the bandwidth. We note, however, that one can define another type of magic angle from the perspective of the effective mass. Specifically, we find that the second derivative of E−​(ky)E_{-}(k_{y}) in Eq. (S18) vanishes at ky=0k_{y}=0 when θ=θc​2\theta=\theta_{c2}, where

θc​2=2​arcsin⁡[32​π​|kqi||kλi|​|mw0|−2m2w0w2cosϕr]≈20.39∘.\theta_{c2}=2\arcsin{\Bigg[\frac{3}{2\pi}\frac{|\textbf{k}_{q_{i}}|}{|\textbf{k}_{\lambda_{i}}|}\sqrt{|mw_{0}|-2m^{2}w_{0}w_{2}\cos\phi_{r}}\Bigg]}\approx 20.39^{\circ}. (S29)

This condition defines a secondary magic angle, at which the leading term in the expansion of E−​(ky)E_{-}(k_{y}) near ky=0k_{y}=0 becomes quartic. Under this circumstance, the density of states exhibits an exact power-law divergence. For details, see Power-law-divergent density of states from the taco band section.

S0.4 Band structure over the whole moiré Brillouin zone

In this section, we discuss the band structure and density of states (DOS) obtained by extending our continuum model beyond the line connecting λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime}. As in Fig. S8, we assume that the interlayer tunneling parameters remain approximately constant as the twist angle varies.

General momentum dependence of the interlayer tunneling— To construct a more general model that covers the whole mBZ, we need to find the form of the interlayer tunneling t⁡(kx,ky)t(k_{x},k_{y}) at a general k. For this we approximate that t⁡(kx,ky)t(k_{x},k_{y}) has a polynomial form:

t⁡(kx,ky)=∑a,b=02Wa​b​(kx−k0​x)a​kyb,t(k_{x},k_{y})=\sum_{a,b=0}^{2}W_{ab}(k_{x}-k_{0x})^{a}k_{y}^{b}, (S30)

where k0​x=[kλ1+kλ2]x/2k_{0x}=[\textbf{k}_{\lambda_{1}}+\textbf{k}_{\lambda_{2}}]_{x}/2 Here, as we assumed quadratic dispersion near the valleys, we cut the series of tt up to the second order in kxk_{x} and kyk_{y}. Due to the three C2​y​TC_{2y}T-type symmetries, any Wa​bW_{ab} with odd bb must be zero:

Wa​b=0​ for b= odd.\displaystyle W_{ab}=0\text{ for $b=$ odd}. (S31)

From the numerical data fitting along the λ−λ′\lambda-\lambda^{\prime} line, we have

W00\displaystyle W_{00} =w0,\displaystyle=w_{0}, (S32)
W02\displaystyle W_{02} =w2.\displaystyle=w_{2}. (S33)

From the fitting along the γ−μ\gamma-\mu line where ky=0k_{y}=0, we find that

W10\displaystyle W_{10} ≈0.0235​a0​ eV,\displaystyle\approx 0.0235a_{0}\text{ eV}, (S34)
W20\displaystyle W_{20} ≈0.0347​a02​ eV.\displaystyle\approx 0.0347a_{0}^{2}\text{ eV}. (S35)

The remaining Wa​bW_{ab} could in principle be obtained from the data fitting along the γ−λ\gamma-\lambda line. However, the lowest-order term with both a≠0a\neq 0 and b≠0b\neq 0 is already cubic (a=1,b=2a=1,b=2) in kxk_{x} and kyk_{y}, is therefore excluded from the model.

The 12-band continuum model Hamiltonian— Our model includes six λi\lambda_{i} points. For each λi\lambda_{i} at kλi≈0.700​kqi\textbf{k}_{\lambda_{i}}\approx 0.700~\textbf{k}_{q_{i}}, there are two valleys, one with spin-up and the other with spin-down. The Hamiltonian reads

H⁡(k)=(H↑​(k)H↓​(k)),H(\textbf{k})=\begin{pmatrix}H_{\uparrow}(\textbf{k})&\\ &H_{\downarrow}(\textbf{k})\end{pmatrix}, (S36)

where

H↑​(k)=(H↑1​(k)t12​(k)0000t12∗​(k)H↑2​(k)000000H↑3​(k)t34​(k)0000t34∗​(k)H↑4​(k)000000H↑5​(k)t56​(k)0000t56∗​(k)H↑6​(k))H_{\uparrow}(\textbf{k})=\begin{pmatrix}H_{\uparrow 1}(\textbf{k})&t_{12}(\textbf{k})&0&0&0&0\\ t_{12}^{*}(\textbf{k})&H_{\uparrow 2}(\textbf{k})&0&0&0&0\\ 0&0&H_{\uparrow 3}(\textbf{k})&t_{34}(\textbf{k})&0&0\\ 0&0&t_{34}^{*}(\textbf{k})&H_{\uparrow 4}(\textbf{k})&0&0\\ 0&0&0&0&H_{\uparrow 5}(\textbf{k})&t_{56}(\textbf{k})\\ 0&0&0&0&t_{56}^{*}(\textbf{k})&H_{\uparrow 6}(\textbf{k})\end{pmatrix} (S37)

and

H↓​(k)=(H↓1​(k)0000t61​(k)0H↓2​(k)t23​(k)0000t23∗​(k)H↓3​(k)000000H↓4​(k)t45​(k)0000t45∗​(k)OPENH↓5​k)0t61∗​(k)0000H↓6​(k).)H_{\downarrow}(\textbf{k})=\begin{pmatrix}H_{\downarrow 1}(\textbf{k})&0&0&0&0&t_{61}(\textbf{k})\\ 0&H_{\downarrow 2}(\textbf{k})&t_{23}(\textbf{k})&0&0&0\\ 0&t_{23}^{*}(\textbf{k})&H_{\downarrow 3}(\textbf{k})&0&0&0\\ 0&0&0&H_{\downarrow 4}(\textbf{k})&t_{45}(\textbf{k})&0\\ 0&0&0&t_{45}^{*}(\textbf{k})&H_{\downarrow 5}\textbf{k})&0\\ t_{61}^{*}(\textbf{k})&0&0&0&0&H_{\downarrow 6}(\textbf{k}).\end{pmatrix} (S38)

Here, Hi​(k)H_{i}(\textbf{k}) includes the kinetic energy and moiré potential of electron near the λi\lambda_{i} valley, and ti​j​(k)t_{ij}(\textbf{k}) is the coupling between the λi\lambda_{i} and λj\lambda_{j} valley due to the interlayer tunneling. The diagonal elements in Eq. S37 and Eq. S38 are given by

H↑i​(k)\displaystyle H_{\uparrow i}{(\textbf{k})} =∑α=x,y[R⁡(−2​⌊(i−1)/2⌋3​π+(−1)i​θ2)​(k−kqi)]α22​mα+A​cos⁡(aqi⋅k+φ),\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha=x,y}\frac{[R(-\frac{2\lfloor(i-1)/2\rfloor}{3}\pi+(-1)^{i}\frac{\theta}{2})(\textbf{k}-\textbf{k}_{q_{i}})]_{\alpha}^{2}}{2m_{\alpha}}+A\cos{(\textbf{a}_{q_{i}}\cdot\textbf{k}+\varphi)}, (S39)

and

H↓i​(k)\displaystyle H_{\downarrow i}{(\textbf{k})} =∑α=x,y[R⁡(1−2​⌊i/2⌋3​π−(−1)i​θ2)​(k−kqi)]α22​mα+A​cos⁡(aqi⋅k+φ),\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha=x,y}\frac{[R(\frac{1-2\lfloor i/2\rfloor}{3}\pi-(-1)^{i}\frac{\theta}{2})(\textbf{k}-\textbf{k}_{q_{i}})]_{\alpha}^{2}}{2m_{\alpha}}+A\cos{(\textbf{a}_{q_{i}}\cdot\textbf{k}+\varphi)}, (S40)

where ai=[R(π/3)](i−1)(a0/sin(θ/2))(−3/4,1/4)\textbf{a}_{i}=[R(\pi/3)]^{(i-1)}(a_{0}/\sin{(\theta/2)})(-\sqrt{3}/4,1/4). The off-diagonal elements in Eq. S37 and Eq. S38 are given by

ti​j​(k)\displaystyle t_{ij}{(\textbf{k})} =w0+w2​ei​ϕr​qi​j,22​(k)+W10​(qi​j,1​(k)−k0​x)+W20​(qi​j,1​(k)−k0​x)2,\displaystyle=w_{0}+w_{2}e^{i\phi_{r}}q_{ij,2}^{2}(\textbf{k})+W_{10}(q_{ij,1}(\textbf{k})-k_{0x})+W_{20}(q_{ij,1}(\textbf{k})-k_{0x})^{2}, (S41)

where

qi​j,1​(k)\displaystyle q_{ij,1}{(\textbf{k})} =k⋅(z^×n^i​j),\displaystyle=\textbf{k}\cdot(\hat{z}\times\hat{n}_{ij}), (S43)
qi​j,2​(k)\displaystyle q_{ij,2}{(\textbf{k})} =k⋅n^i​j,\displaystyle=\textbf{k}\cdot\hat{n}_{ij}, (S44)
n^i​j\displaystyle\hat{n}_{ij} ≡kλj−kλi|kλj−kλi|.\displaystyle\equiv\frac{\textbf{k}_{\lambda_{j}}-\textbf{k}_{\lambda_{i}}}{|\textbf{k}_{\lambda_{j}}-\textbf{k}_{\lambda_{i}}|}. (S45)

We note that q12,1​(k)=kxq_{12,1}(\textbf{k})=k_{x} and q12,2​(k)=kyq_{12,2}(\textbf{k})=k_{y}.

S0.5 Taco band structure

Fig. S10a shows the band structure obtained along the γ−λ′−λ−κ\gamma-\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda-\kappa path. Compared to the first-principles results, the model calculation reproduces well the dispersion of the lowest-energy bands of H↑​(k)H_{\uparrow}(\textbf{k}) and H↓​(k)H_{\downarrow}(\textbf{k}) around the λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime} points. However, it underestimates the bandwidths of the second and third bands, while overestimating the bandwidths of higher bands. This discrepancy arises because the higher-energy bands originate from different λi\lambda_{i} valleys than those chosen as λ\lambda and λ′\lambda^{\prime}, and the polynomial approximation of the Hamiltonian, truncated at second order in momentum, introduces errors at momenta far from the valleys. Fig. S10b shows the energy spectrum of the taco band. Here, “taco” refers to the fact that along the edges of the hexagon formed by the λi\lambda_{i} points, the band dispersion is nearly flat, while it is quadratic in the perpendicular direction, resembling the shape of a folded taco.

Power-law-divergent density of states from the taco band— The DOS shown in Fig. 5d of the main text is computed from

D⁡(E)\displaystyle D(E) =1N​∑i=112∑k∈mBZδ⁡(E−εi​(k))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{12}\sum_{\textbf{k}\in\textrm{mBZ}}\delta(E-\varepsilon_{i}(\textbf{k}))
≈1π​N​∑i=112∑k∈mBZη(E−εi​(k))2+η2,\displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{\pi N}\sum_{i=1}^{12}\sum_{\textbf{k}\in\textrm{mBZ}}\frac{\eta}{(E-\varepsilon_{i}(\textbf{k}))^{2}+\eta^{2}}, (S46)

where εi​(k)\varepsilon_{i}(\textbf{k}) denote the ii-th eigenvalue of H⁡(k)H(\textbf{k}) in Eq. S36 and NN is the system size. To numerically calculate DOS, we introduce a small broadening factor η\eta. We find that the DOS of magic-angle twisted bilayer WSe22 exhibits a divergence near the energy of the taco band. This divergence originates from a van Hove singularity (vHS) [15], corresponding to a saddle point in the band dispersion located at the midpoint of the λ\lambda–λ′\lambda^{\prime} line with energy E−​(0)E_{-}(0). Consequently, the DOS D⁡(E)D(E) diverges logarithmically, D⁡(E)∝−log10⁡(E−E−​(0))D(E)\propto-\log_{10}(E-E_{-}(0)) in the vicinity of E−​(0)E_{-}(0). However, this strictly logarithmic behavior is visible only within an extremely narrow energy window set by the taco band’s bandwidth. At larger energy scales, the DOS instead appears to follow an approximate power-law divergence, D⁡(E)∝(E−E−​(0))−aD(E)\propto(E-E_{-}(0))^{-a}.

This power-law divergence originates from the quasi-one-dimensional (1D) nature of the taco band. In 1D, a vHS corresponds to an extremum in the band dispersion, and it leads to a power-law divergence of the DOS. Along the λ\lambda–λ′\lambda^{\prime} lines, the taco band is nearly flat in one direction while it exhibits a minimum in the other direction, making it effectively a quasi-1D vHS. Notably, the exponent aa of DOS in Fig. 5e of the main text is smaller than the ideal 1D value of 1/21/2. This is because the taco band remains quasi-1D flat only along short line segments, while becoming dispersive away from the λ\lambda–λ′\lambda^{\prime} line. To capture this, we consider the model dispersion

ε⁡(k)=ε0+a​kx2+b​ky2+c​kyp,\varepsilon(\textbf{k})=\varepsilon_{0}+ak_{x}^{2}+bk_{y}^{2}+ck_{y}^{p}, (S47)

with pp an even integer larger than 2. The DOS is then

D⁡(Δ​E)\displaystyle D(\Delta E) =∫d2​k(2​π)2​δ​(E−ε⁡(k))\displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{2}k}{(2\pi)^{2}}\delta(E-\varepsilon(\textbf{k}))
=1(2​π)2​∫−∞∞d​ky​Θ⁡(Δ​E−b​ky2−c​kyp)a⁡(Δ​E−b​ky2−c​kyp),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dk_{y}\frac{\Theta(\Delta E-bk_{y}^{2}-ck_{y}^{p})}{\sqrt{a(\Delta E-bk_{y}^{2}-ck_{y}^{p})}}, (S48)

where Δ​E=E−ε0\Delta E=E-\varepsilon_{0} and Θ\Theta is the Heaviside step function. Different parameter choices yield distinct types of singularities. When b=c=0b=c=0, the dispersion is perfectly 1D, and D⁡(Δ​E)∝1/Δ​ED(\Delta E)\propto 1/\sqrt{\Delta E}. For b≫c>0b\gg c>0, the DOS does not diverge. For b<0b<0, (kx,ky)=(0,0)(k_{x},k_{y})=(0,0) becomes a saddle point, giving a logarithmic divergence, D⁡(Δ​E)∝−log10⁡Δ​ED(\Delta E)\propto-\log_{10}\Delta E. For b=0b=0 and c>0c>0, one finds D⁡(Δ​E)∝(Δ​E)−(1/2−1/p)D(\Delta E)\propto(\Delta E)^{-(1/2-1/p)}; in particular, for p=4p=4, the DOS diverges with exponent 1/41/4. Thus, depending on bb, cc, and pp, the DOS at Δ​E=0\Delta E=0 exhibits either no divergence, logarithmic divergence, or a power-law divergence with exponent less than 1/21/2. For small negative bb and positive cc, the divergence is intermediate between logarithmic and the 1/41/4 power law. This explains why quasi-1D band structures, such as the taco band, can exhibit approximate power-law divergences with exponents significantly smaller than 1/21/2. Fig. S11 shows D⁡(Δ​E)D(\Delta E) vs. log10⁡Δ​E\log_{10}\Delta E and log10⁡D⁡(Δ​E)\log_{10}D(\Delta E) vs. log10⁡Δ​E\log_{10}\Delta E graphs for different bb and cc values with a=1a=1 and p=4p=4. For aa, bb, and cc extracted from the saddle point in the dispersion of the Hamiltonian in Eq. (S36) with p=4p=4, the log10⁡D⁡(Δ​E)\log_{10}D(\Delta E) vs. log10⁡Δ​E\log_{10}\Delta E plot appears linear at larger energy scales, whereas the D⁡(Δ​E)D(\Delta E) vs. log10⁡Δ​E\log_{10}\Delta E plot becomes linear at smaller energy scales. This crossover behavior is consistent with the DOS calculated from the model Hamiltonian in Eq. (S36), and the estimated crossover energy scale, Δ​E≈0.3\Delta E\approx 0.3 meV, shows good agreement between the two results.

Finally, we comment on the dependence of the DOS on the twist angle θ\theta, the broadening factor η\eta, and the nature of the divergence at the secondary magic angle. Fig. S12 shows the log–log DOS at several twist angles near 21.8∘21.8^{\circ}, computed with η=0.1\eta=0.1 meV. For θ∼21∘\theta\sim 21^{\circ}, no clear divergence is observed, although a peak structure in the DOS is already visible. As θ\theta increases, the peak sharpens, and once θ>21.4∘\theta>21.4^{\circ}, the midpoint of the λ\lambda–λ′\lambda^{\prime} line evolves into a saddle point. The DOS reaches its maximum near θ=21.7∘\theta=21.7^{\circ}–21.8∘21.8^{\circ}, where the taco-band bandwidth is minimized. For larger θ\theta, however, the energy window supporting approximate power-law divergence shrinks.

Numerically, the secondary magic angle—defined by the vanishing effective mass at the midpoint of the λ\lambda–λ′\lambda^{\prime} line—is found to be θc​2≈21.35∘\theta_{c2}\approx 21.35^{\circ}, slightly larger than the analytic prediction of Eq. (S29). This secondary magic angle acts as a critical point: for smaller θ\theta, a finite DOS peak exists without true divergence, while for larger θ\theta, a van Hove singularity emerges accompanied by an extremely large effective mass along one direction.

From theory, the predicted divergence exponent at the secondary magic angle is −1/4-1/4, since the dispersion follows a quartic form in momentum near the band minimum. In the calculations above, however, the observed divergence at the secondary magic angle is even weaker than at the primary magic angle, primarily due to the finite broadening factor. As illustrated in Fig. S12, the DOS at θ=21.35∘\theta=21.35^{\circ} with much smaller broadening factor η=0.002\eta=0.002 meV indeed exhibits a power-law divergence with exponent close to −1/4-1/4 at very low energies, but this behavior is rapidly cut off once Δ​E\Delta E approaches the broadening scale. We further note that the energy range of approximate power-law scaling is much wider at θ=21.8∘\theta=21.8^{\circ} than at θ=21.35∘\theta=21.35^{\circ}. This happens because the quartic (ky4k_{y}^{4}) approximation to the dispersion is valid only within a limited momentum window. At larger kyk_{y}, the dispersion crosses over to quadratic behavior. Near the primary magic angle, the flattening extends over a broader momentum range, thereby sustaining the ky4k_{y}^{4} approximation across a wider energy window. In contrast, near the secondary magic angle, the dispersion may locally resemble a ky4k_{y}^{4} form almost perfectly, but only over a very narrow kyk_{y}-range. As a result, the effective power-law scaling breaks down much more quickly, limiting the observable regime for divergence.

To better capture the behavior of the taco band over a larger energy range, one can consider a dispersion of the form

ε⁡(𝐤)=a​kx2+b​ky2​tanh2⁡(β​ky).\varepsilon(\mathbf{k})=ak_{x}^{2}+bk_{y}^{2}\tanh^{2}(\beta k_{y}). (S49)

For small kyk_{y}, tanh⁡(β​ky)≈β​ky\tanh(\beta k_{y})\approx\beta k_{y}, yielding a quartic dependence on kyk_{y} (ε⁡(𝐤)≈a​kx2+c​ky4\varepsilon(\mathbf{k})\approx ak_{x}^{2}+ck_{y}^{4} with c=b​β2c=b\beta^{2}). For large kyk_{y}, tanh⁡(β​ky)≈1\tanh(\beta k_{y})\approx 1, recovering a quadratic dispersion along kyk_{y} (ε⁡(𝐤)≈a​kx2+b​ky2\varepsilon(\mathbf{k})\approx ak_{x}^{2}+bk_{y}^{2}). This model therefore captures the crossover from quartic to quadratic behavior and mimics the taco-band dispersion of our system over a larger energy window. Fig. S14a shows the band dispersions from a​kx2+b​ky2​tanh2⁡(β​ky)ak_{x}^{2}+bk_{y}^{2}\tanh^{2}(\beta k_{y}) with parameters a≈0.545777a\approx 0.545777, b≈1.5b\approx 1.5, and β≈1.3\beta\approx 1.3. Fig. S14b presents the corresponding DOS from the analytic dispersion, which reproduces both the divergent exponent and the energy range of divergence seen in the full model. Since the DOS from the full model Hamiltonian is normalized differently (with units of eV-1/unit cell/atom), we applied an overall multiplicative constant to align the two curves for visual comparison.
